name: Borth coastal defence reef (incl. Wallog headland)
year: Feasibility study May 2004 [R10][R4]; design from Oct 2009 [R1][R4]; construction started Jan 2011 [R1]; contractor's target completion Nov 2011 [R1][R9]; Coflein gives completion March 2012 [R3]; wider Phase-1 scheme described as 2011-2015 [R6] Blacka et al. (2013, p.70) also state completion in 2012 [R14].
type: Submerged rock (riprap) multi-purpose reef plus rock groynes, breakwaters and beach nourishment [R1][R4]. AUDIT NOTE 2026-10-10: 'submerged' holds only at high water. Design crest levels (drawings 9V5090/1020-1023 rev C1) are +0.50 mODN for the surf-reef arm (northern 'boot') and +1.50 mODN for the shore-parallel oval, which is a breakwater, not a surf reef [R16]; mean sea level is about +0.31 mODN (mean of the four SMP2 levels MHWS +2.56, MHWN +1.06, MLWN -0.64, MLWS -1.74 mODN; our computation, +-0.15 m) [R18], so the reef-arm crest is about 0.2 m above MSL and the rock is bare at low tide (Esri image of 2024-09-17, rock bare; 2012-10-27, awash) [R19]
purpose: Primary: flood and erosion protection for Borth village, built on a mobile shingle bank whose 1970s timber-groyne defences were failing [R1][R2][R4]. Secondary/amenity: shape the reef so breaking swell also creates a surf wave, because the community explicitly rejected a hard sea wall in favour of keeping an open beach [R1][R2][R4]
size: Reef sited c.400 m offshore per the contractor (2011) [R1] / c.300 m per local/heritage sources (2013 press, Coflein) [R2][R3]; 275,000 t total material moved (84,500 t shingle replacement, 18,500 t Type-3 rock 0.3-1t, 16,200 t Type-1 rock 3-6t, 42,000 t Type-4 rock 6-10t, 500 t Type-6 rock 5-100kg) [R1]; Coflein separately states c.300,000 t of rock for the whole works [R3] SOURCES DISAGREE on distance offshore: contractor c.400 m [R1], local/heritage c.300 m [R2][R3], but Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2 p.66) give 110 m (north reef) and 140 m (south reef), probably measured to the undisturbed shoreline [R14]. Blacka also gives two reefs of rubble mound: north reef 72 m (longshore) x 170 m (cross-shore), south reef 85 m x 45 m (max dims), depth 4.0 m, crest at MSL [R14]. Typical tide range 6.0 m in Blacka Table 4.3 (p.68; term not defined) vs the card's spring range 4.7-4.8 m [R11]; both kept. Project-traced outline (not a published figure): northern mound 144.9 m long, 27.6 m mean width; southern oval 71.8 x 31.0 m; centroid of both mounds 330.5 m offshore (nearest edge 257 m, farthest 397 m), traced from the Esri image of 2024-09-17 [R19]; this differs from Blacka's rectangles (72 x 170 m, 85 x 45 m) [R14], which are maximum dimensions of an unspecified outline.
cost: Figures vary by source, not reconciled: Phase 1 funding envelope GBP 7M (FY2009/10-2010/11) [R4]; GBP 13.5M "first phase of the strategy" quoted in 2009 [R1]; BAM Nuttall's winning construction tender GBP 11.5M [R1]; full phased scheme costed at GBP 29M in 2011-2013 press [R1][R2]; Coflein gives completed reef/coastal-defence works at GBP 13M [R3]; Wikipedia gives GBP 12M for the 2011-2015 scheme [R6]
cost_usd_approx: ASSUMPTION (conversion made by this project, not by a source): at the 2013 average of about US$1.56 per GBP (0.6391 GBP per USD, CIA World Factbook via IndexMundi, 2013 value only; other years not confirmed) [R20], GBP 12-13M is about US$19-20M and GBP 29M about US$45M. Corrected 2026-10-10: the earlier text (US$15-17M and US$36M at 'rates of ~1.25-1.6') was unsourced and its low rate end (1.25) is below any 2011-2013 rate; use as order of magnitude only
financed_by: Coast Protection Grant from the Welsh Assembly Government (later Welsh Government) and Convergence funding from the Welsh European Funding Office (WEFO) / European Regional Development Fund [R4][R6]
motivation: Borth sits on a mobile shingle bank in Cardigan Bay; its 1970s timber groyne and breastwork sea defences were judged inadequate, with ordinary storms causing overtopping flooding through homes, per Borth councillor Ray Quant [R2]. A council feasibility study found existing defences within 10 years of failure with potentially catastrophic losses possible, triggering a 150-resident 2001 visioning meeting [R4]. Ceredigion County Council's coast and rivers engineer, Rhodri Llwyd, said the scheme had been 15 years in the making and that the community absolutely didn't want a wall, so the idea of a reef was born [R1][R2]
designer: Royal Haskoning (detailed design, appointed Oct 2009); specialist reef designer ASR (sub-consultant); physical modelling by HR Wallingford; environmental consultant Atkins [R1][R4]. Original feasibility study "Borth Multi-Purpose reef for Coastal Protection and Amenity" completed May 2004 for Ceredigion County Council (authors not confirmed; ResearchGate record blocked, content corroborated via Borth Community website) [R10][R4]
contractor: BAM Nuttall (site agent Ray Jones); plant from Norton Plant Hire [R1][R4]
status_now: Built and in service; as of December 2011 residents reported the new defences had already stopped two high tides from flooding their properties [R2][R3]. The wider Borth-to-Ynyslas coastal-protection programme was still being planned/phased in later business-case documents, implying more phases beyond the reef itself continued years after Phase 1 (details not found) [R4]
hover_text: A c.300-400 m offshore multi-purpose rock reef plus groynes and beach nourishment, built 2011-2012 for roughly GBP 12-13M (reported up to GBP 29M for the full phased scheme), financed by Welsh Government and EU (WEFO/ERDF) funding; it stopped flooding within months of substantial completion, but years later the surf-industry press still describes Borth only as "a proposed" reef site rather than crediting it with a reliable wave [R1][R2][R3][R7].
design_as_planned: The preferred option, chosen after comparing technical, economic, amenity, environmental and safety criteria, was "Rock Beach Control Structures with a Multi-Purpose Reef and Beach Nourishment" [R4][R10]. Phase 1 combined: a submerged multi-purpose reef near the Craig y Delyn cliffs at the beach's southern end (sited there so the community could keep an open beach and unobstructed views), two rock groynes and two rock breakwaters further along the frontage to retain shingle, and beach nourishment (originally 150,000 m3 of imported shingle) [R1][R4]. Designed to a 1-in-100-year storm standard while remaining adaptable to future climate change [R4]. The reef's role was explicitly dual: reduce wave energy to protect the beach from erosion and broaden the beach inshore, while also being shaped to help swell waves break as a secondary surfing amenity [R1][R2]. The team settled on "Option 9A" for outline design after comparing numerous layouts, with 3D physical wave-basin modelling by HR Wallingford used to size the rock armour [R1]
as_built_vs_design: Construction followed the planned reef/groynes/breakwaters/nourishment layout, but with two contractor-driven, budget-closing changes: the client's design already carried about GBP 1M of cost overrun after physical-model testing showed extra rock was needed, and BAM Nuttall's tender then came in a further GBP 1M over that inflated budget [R1]. BAM Nuttall closed the combined c.GBP 2M gap by (1) mining and reusing the beach's own existing shingle, bulked up with cheaper imported quarried material underneath and the original shingle put back on top, instead of importing the full 150,000 m3 specified, and (2) building a temporary rock causeway out to the reef site so land-based excavators and dumper trucks could be used instead of the originally tendered floating marine plant [R1]. The causeway was intended to be removed once the reef was finished [R9]. Construction ran on a tight tidal window (6am-9pm with a three-hour high-tide stoppage), with over 8,000 material deliveries made by September 2011 [R1][R2]
outcome: Coastal protection: residents reported the new defences had already stopped two high tides from flooding their properties by December 2011, while the works were still substantially under construction [R2][R3]. An unplanned side effect of the earthworks was the exposure of a prehistoric submerged forest (oak, pine, birch, willow and hazel stumps dated to roughly 1500 BCE) tied to the Welsh legend of Cantre'r Gwaelod, now visible at low tide [R6]. Surfing outcome is contested: press coverage at construction time promised the reef would provide excellent surf conditions and boost the local economy [R2], but the Stormrider Surf Guide, years after completion, still describes Borth as merely "a proposed" artificial reef site rather than a functioning named surf break [R7], and Surf-Forecast.com rates Borth's surf quality only 3.0/5 with beginner difficulty and no posted first-hand surfer reviews [R8]. No wave-height, ride-length or surfable-days measurement for the reef was found [R7][R8] Blacka et al. (2013, p.70): performance 'yet to be determined' (completed 2012); protection and surfing rated 'unknown (insufficient monitoring)' (Table 4.1); Fig 4.1 (p.72) shows the reef in June 2012 [R14].
why_worked_or_failed: For coastal protection, the scheme functioned successfully in its early years, withstanding December-2011 storms without flooding the properties it protects within months of substantial completion [R2][R3]. Credited design choices: graded, multi-tonne rock armour (up to 10 t pieces) sized via HR Wallingford's 3D physical modelling before construction rather than off-the-shelf sizing [R1]; a reef+groyne+breakwater system working with beach nourishment instead of a rigid sea wall, chosen because the community rejected a wall [R1][R2]; and a construction sequencing (temporary causeway, tidal work windows) that let the contractor place rock accurately below the high-tide line [R1]. For the surfing function, no source found explains in engineering terms (crest depth, slope, wave-focusing geometry) why the wave has or hasn't performed; the continued "proposed" framing in the Stormrider guide is suggestive the amenity function has not been widely recognised as delivering a notable wave, but no direct technical post-mortem was located [R7]
unexpected_results: The exposure of the prehistoric petrified forest and its tie-in to the Cantre'r Gwaelod legend was an unplanned, publicised side effect of the earthworks [R6]. No sources found document fishing-pressure changes, ecological studies, rip-current safety incidents, litigation, or measurable tourism-economy impact specifically tied to the Borth reef (treated as a genuine gap, not confirmed absence of any such effect)
could_be_better: No source located offers an explicit engineers'/authors' retrospective critique of the Borth scheme's design or execution (unlike, e.g., Boscombe's published post-mortem). The one available critical signal is indirect: the Stormrider Surf Guide's continued description of Borth as merely "a proposed artificial reef site" years after completion implies the reef has not become a recognised, reliably rideable wave in the way pre-construction press promised [R7]; Surf-Forecast's low consistency/quality scores point the same way [R8], though neither source explains which design choice is responsible. From a cost-management perspective, the construction tender came in over budget on top of a design that had already grown by about GBP 1M after physical-model testing, and the contractor had to redesign its construction method and material sourcing specifically to close that gap, implying the original budget/design had under-priced the works as first specified [R1]
relevance_to_israel: Cardigan Bay/Aberystwyth (immediately adjacent to Borth) is macrotidal: spring tidal range is roughly 4.7-4.8 m (high spring tide c.5.4 m, low tide down to c.0.6 m) [R11]. This is drastically larger than the Israeli Mediterranean coast (Haifa/Ashkelon/Netanya etc.), which is effectively microtidal, with a tidal range on the order of tens of centimetres. A reef crest depth and rock-armour design tuned by HR Wallingford's physical modelling to work across a c.4.7 m tidal swing at Borth [R1] cannot be reused as-is on Israel's coast, since the same structure would sit permanently near a single water level in Israel rather than alternately surfacing and submerging by several metres, changing both wave-breaking performance and exposure/maintenance regime. What transfers conceptually: the core political lesson that a community explicitly chose a submerged multi-purpose reef over a hard sea wall specifically to keep an open, usable beach and views [R1][R2][R4], directly analogous to debates around geotubes/breakwaters at Ashkelon and Netanya. The value-engineering lesson (reusing existing shingle instead of full import, to control cost) is also directly transferable regardless of tidal regime [R1] Tidal range cross-check: the SMP2 Aberystwyth levels give a spring range (MHWS minus MLWS) of 2.56 - (-1.74) = 4.30 m [R18], versus 4.7-4.8 m from Tide-Forecast.com [R11] and 6.0 m in Blacka Table 4.3 [R14]; three different definitions/sources, none preferred here.
